extracted.intended_audience: readers of Montaigne and educated general readers interested in moral/philosophical reflections on love and conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance and evaluative maxims about courtship, modesty, moderation, consent, and age-appropriate sexual behavior drawn from Montaigne's moral essay. The page offers prescriptions about how lovers and the moderately aged ought to behave and judge pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid self-denaturing asceticism
rubrics_metrics.description: One ought not invent additional miseries for oneself by deliberate self-denaturing practices (extreme fasting, cutting, withdrawing from company) that make natural delights shameful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne criticizes fanatic people who 'value themselves upon their contempt of themselves' and who 'purport to grow better by being worse.' He warns that we already have enough inevitable inconveniences and should not increase them 'by th[e] own invention.' Examples: men who only eat once a week, mangle their faces, or never speak to anyone. Aim to live according to natural, not fantastical, rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not prioritize artificial scruples over natural duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid letting particular, provincial or invented rules occupy you at the expense of universal laws of nature, God, and the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne observes that people 'stick to thy own special and fantastic rules' while 'the laws of thy parish occupy and bind thee: those of God and the world concern thee not.' The counsel is to attend first to essential, natural duties rather than innumerable superficial obligations that dissipate moral attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware deceptive modesty (partial disclosure as treachery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Half-expressed modesty or partial concealment that leads others to imagine more than is intended is dishonest and can be more offensive than frankness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne: 'He who is afraid to express himself, draws us on to guess at more than is meant; there is treachery in this sort of modesty.' Examples: people who hide only to show, or those who expose just enough to invite the imagination. Avoid calculated ambiguity that manipulates another's imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use gradation and delay in bestowing favours
rubrics_metrics.description: Restraint, delay and progressive steps in courtship increase desire and make conquest more honourable and pleasurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne 'commends a gradation and delay in bestowing their favours.' He compares the approach to moving through 'porticoes and passages, long and pleasant galleries, and many windings.' He argues that 'without hope and without desire we proceed not worth a pin.' Apply measured advances rather than instant surrender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote modesty, discretion, and reputation even if conscience is loose
rubrics_metrics.description: Even those who care little for conscience should maintain a fair outside—modesty and discretion preserve reputation and social order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne advises: 'let her who has no care of her conscience have yet some regard to her reputation; and though she be rotten within, let her carry a fair outside at least.' The point is practical: preserve public decorum to avoid needless scandal and harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value coyness and measured elusiveness in love
rubrics_metrics.description: Coyness and a measured secrecy in the beloved's behaviour are more alluring than immediate openness; 'they better conquer us by flying.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne praises the 'more respectful, more timorous, more coy' love of Spaniards and Italians and recommends that women 'still fly before us, even those who have most mind to be overtaken.' Use temperate reserve as a social and erotic strategy rather than blunt availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminate between physical gratification and true affection (consent matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Loving a body without its consent or desire is not true love; the will and consent of the beloved are essential to genuine affection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne: 'we love a body without a soul or sentiment when we love a body without its consent and desire.' He likens such passion to madness and rejects enjoyment devoid of reciprocal will. Evaluate whether favors reflect real affection or merely physical access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge favours for their motive — beware pleasures obtained for other causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all favors indicate affection; some are given for payment, vanity, revenge, or other motives and may conceal treachery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne warns that 'a thousand other causes besides good-will may procure us this favour from the ladies; this is not a sufficient testimony of affection: treachery may lurk there.' Examine context and motive: is the act freely given or bought, coerced, or instrumental?

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not accept pity-based or socially coerced intimacies
rubrics_metrics.description: Intimacies obtained from pity or social compulsion (e.g., because a suitor is well-attended) are demeaning and not worth pursuing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne criticises the custom forcing women to kiss courtiers with many footmen: 'for three beautiful women we must kiss fifty ugly ones.' He says if kindness comes only from pity, 'I had much rather die than live upon charity.' Prefer mutual esteem over charity-based affection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect a partner's reputation by discreet arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange meetings and conduct affairs in ways that minimize public scandal and discharge risk from the partner's honor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne states he 'have ever, as much as I could, wholly taken upon myself alone the hazard of our assignations' and contrived meetings 'after the hardest and most unusual manner, as less suspected.' Discretion is a duty to those you love: choose methods that shield their position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sparing with promises and faithful where you vow
rubrics_metrics.description: Make few promises but keep them conscientiously; better a few sincere commitments than many empty ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne: 'I have been so sparing of my promises... they have found me faithful.' He frames conscientious fidelity as preferable to rash vows—act with measured pledge-making and uphold obligations you undertake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match sexual ambition to one's age and capacities
rubrics_metrics.description: Older men should not pretend youthful vigour or pursue youthful pleasures that make them ridiculous; accept age-appropriate moderation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne deplores an old man strutting over an inch of vigour 'with as much eagerness as if it could do mighty feats.' He counsels to 'trust not to its seconding that indefatigable... ardour you think in you' and suggests redirecting passions to correspondingly suitable partners. Avoid humiliating displays of misplaced appetite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer pleasures that restore or sustain rather than amplify appetites
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose pleasurable activities that satisfy bodily needs without stirring voracious new desires; avoid pleasures that increase appetite and lead to excess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophy 'ingeniously warns us not to stir up hunger by saturity; not to stuff, instead of merely filling, the belly.' Montaigne recommends pleasures that 'simply satisfy the body's need' and cautions against those that 'may bring us to want.' Especially in old age, pick measured pleasures that revive vigour without causing harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow the mind to moderate and, when appropriate, enhance bodily pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures are not purely corporeal or purely spiritual; the mind can legitimately cultivate pleasures (particularly in weakened bodies) to restore cheerfulness and health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that 'it is rather her [the mind's] part... to hatch and cherish them' and that in a body 'broken with age' it is excusable to 'warm and support it by art, and by the mediation of the fancy.' Use imagination judiciously to make appropriate pleasures sweeter and restorative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ingratitude, treachery, malice and cruelty in pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: Even while indulging in love or licentiousness, do not resort to treachery, ingratitude, malice or cruelty; keep humanity and duty intact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne insists that in his conduct he tolerated 'debauch and licentiousness; but, as to ingratitude, treachery, malice, and cruelty, never.' Pleasure should not be purchased at the expense of fundamental moral decency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation over total abstinence—pleasure as a salutary spice
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy prescribes moderation, not total abstinence; moderate love can refresh the mind and body and be salutary if kept within bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne: 'Philosophy does not contend against natural pleasures, provided they be moderate, and only preaches moderation, not a total abstinence.' He recommends love to 'restore vigilance, sobriety, grace,' and to 'defer the approaches of age' when used wisely and moderately.
